concepts.def: A d-block element that forms at least one stable ion with a partially filled d subshell.
Transition metals form ions in several oxidation states due to similar energies of 4s and 3d electrons.
Central metal ion surrounded by ligands forming dative bonds; e.g. [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺.
Molecule or ion with a lone pair that donates to form a dative bond with a metal centre.
Arise from d-d electron transitions absorbing specific wavelengths of visible light.
Variable oxidation states allow transition metals (e.g. Fe in Haber, V₂O₅ in contact process) to act as catalysts.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Physical Chemistry & Transition Elements — a core area of A-Level Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Physical Chemistry & Transition Elements brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Physical Chemistry & Transition Elements.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Why are transition metal complexes often coloured?
options: s-p transitions
d-d transitions
p-d transitions
Charge separation

mcqs.q: Which is NOT classed as a transition metal by the d-electron criterion?
options: Cu
Fe
Zn
Mn

mcqs.q: Why are most transition metal complex ions coloured?
options: Transition metal ions are coloured because they have a half-full d-subshell which naturally absorbs light.
Transition metals have variable oxidation states because they can gain protons easily.
Ligands split the d-orbitals into two energy levels; electrons absorb visible light to jump between them (d-d transitions), and the complementary colour is transmitted.
Transition metals are coloured because their nuclei emit photons in the visible range.

mcqs.q: Why can transition metals show variable oxidation states?
options: Heterogeneous catalysts are consumed; homogeneous catalysts are not.
The 4s and 3d orbitals are similar in energy, so different numbers of electrons can be removed without a large energy cost.
Transition metals have variable oxidation states because they can gain protons easily.
Transition metals have variable oxidation states because they have many shells of electrons.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes a heterogeneous from a homogeneous catalyst?
options: Transition metals have variable oxidation states because they can gain protons easily.
Heterogeneous catalysts are solid and homogeneous catalysts are liquid — full stop.
Heterogeneous catalysts are consumed; homogeneous catalysts are not.
A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase from the reactants; a homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase.
